context: Current closing price of Palo Alto Networks (PANW): $322.32 USD as of 2026-07-28.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent observed price around 322–323, with each successive horizon projecting slightly higher values. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, expecting minimal movement given typical short-term mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 325, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run equity market trends. At the one-month horizon, I moved to 330, incorporating a modest equity risk premium over time while acknowledging that the asset — likely an equity index or ETF — tends to appreciate gradually in the absence of shocks.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each horizon. Daily volatility in broad equity markets typically runs around 0.8–1.2%, which translates to a roughly ±1.9% band at one day — consistent with my ±12.5 point interval around 323.5. As the horizon extends, uncertainty compounds, so the one-week interval widens to roughly ±21 points and the one-month interval widens further to ±42 points. These widths reflect realized volatility scaling approximately with the square root of time, a standard assumption when no specific volatility regime shift is anticipated.

There are several risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise inflation print, weaker-than-expected employment figures, or unexpected central bank hawkishness — could drive prices well below 311 even within a single day. Geopolitical escalation or a liquidity event in credit markets could produce tail moves beyond the one-month lower bound of 288. On the upside, a strongly dovish policy pivot, blowout earnings surprises, or a rapid de-escalation of geopolitical risk could push prices above 372 over the monthly horizon.

It's also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions with no fat-tail adjustments beyond what's embedded in the historical volatility estimate. In reality, equity returns exhibit excess kurtosis and negative skew, meaning the true probability of extreme downside outcomes is somewhat higher than my symmetric intervals imply. Sudden volatility regime changes — such as those seen during the 2020 COVID shock or the 2022 rate-hiking cycle — could render even the one-week interval far too narrow.
